stem: After discharge, a former patient sends the nurse a friend request on the nurse's personal social-media account. Which response best aligns with professional-boundary guidance?

options.A: Accept the request because discharge automatically removes professional-boundary concerns.
options.B: Accept the request if the former patient initiated the contact, because the nurse is then not responsible for the boundary.
options.C: Decline personal online social contact and maintain the professional boundary, following applicable employer policy and nursing-regulatory guidance.
options.D: Decline the friend request but offer a personal phone number instead because private texting is outside social-media boundary guidance.

rationale: NCSBN guidance requires nurses to maintain professional boundaries in electronic media and specifically advises caution with online social contact involving patients or former patients. Current NCSBN boundary resources also recognize gratifying personal relationships with current or former clients as potential boundary violations. A patient or former patient initiating contact does not transfer the nurse's responsibility to maintain the professional boundary, and moving the personal contact from social media to private texting does not remove the underlying boundary concern.
educational_objective: Maintain professional boundaries with former patients in electronic communication by declining personal social contact and following applicable employer and nursing-regulatory guidance.
source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
source_document_title: Professional Boundaries; A Nurse's Guide to the Use of Social Media; A Nurse's Guide to Professional Boundaries

source_original.stem: After discharge, a former patient sends the nurse a friend request on a personal social-media account. Which response best aligns with professional-boundary guidance?

options.A: Accept the request because discharge ends the professional relationship and therefore removes boundary concerns.
options.B: Accept the request if the former patient initiated it, because initiation transfers responsibility for the boundary.
options.C: Maintain the professional boundary and decline personal online social contact, following employer and board guidance.
options.D: Decline the friend request but offer a personal phone number instead because private texting is outside boundary rules.

source_original.rationale: NCSBN advises maintaining professional boundaries in electronic media and using caution with online social contact with patients and former patients. A patient initiating contact does not automatically make a personal relationship appropriate. The safest response is to preserve the professional boundary and follow employer and board-of-nursing guidance.
source_original.source_detail: NCSBN — Professional Boundaries / Social Media: maintain professional boundaries in electronic communication and use caution with current/former patient social relationships; patient initiation does not remove boundary risk. Current NCSBN professional-boundaries guidance at exact URL; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Safe and Effective Care Environment — Management of Care; Assignment, Delegation and Supervision; prioritization/continuity/client rights as applicable. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Retained the professional-boundary construct and key. Tightened the wording so discharge and patient initiation are not treated as automatic legal rules, and generalized the response to applicable employer and nursing-regulatory guidance. Recalibrated difficulty from hard to medium because current NCSBN guidance makes the governing principle direct once the former-patient nuance is recognized.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Professional boundaries — social media and former patients
audit_findings.source_authority: Official current NCSBN professional-boundaries and social-media resources.
audit_findings.currentness: NCSBN lists 2024 editions of both relevant brochures; resource pages rechecked 2026-08-16.
audit_findings.exact_locator: NCSBN boundaries/social-media sections directly cover electronic professional boundaries and former-patient social contact; NCSBN discipline guidance confirms current/former-client personal relationships can present boundary violations.
audit_findings.claim_audit: Final item does not claim every former-patient contact is universally illegal; it asks for the best professional-boundary response and preserves jurisdiction/employer-policy context.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because discharge does not automatically eliminate boundary risk.
distractor_audit.B: Incorrect because the nurse retains responsibility for professional boundaries regardless of who initiates contact.
distractor_audit.C: Uniquely consistent with NCSBN's caution and boundary-maintenance guidance.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because changing the communication channel does not eliminate the personal-boundary issue.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only C preserves the professional boundary without relying on an unsupported automatic exception.
audit_findings.cueing: All options are plausible responses to the same online-boundary scenario.
audit_findings.blueprint: Fits NCSBN Management of Care ethical/professional responsibility and client-rights content.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Adversarial review confirmed the final wording avoids overclaiming a universal statutory prohibition while still testing the clear NCSBN professional-boundary standard.
